papers.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

papers.title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.

papers.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
papers.abstract_en: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

papers.title: ParGLU: Partial Gating Improves Language Modeling in MoE Transformers
papers.abstract_en: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.

papers.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
papers.abstract_en: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

papers.title: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
papers.abstract_en: Phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Phase-OTDR) enables distributed vibration sensing, but reliable event classification has traditionally relied on fully supervised models that require extensive annotated data. This study examines the adaptability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for Phase-OTDR event recognition through few-shot learning. Raw samples are converted into Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped and resized to RGB images, and processed by a Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) image encoder; few-shot adaptation optimizes only the Tip-Adapter-F cache keys, leaving both encoders unchanged. Under a leakage-controlled protocol (train-side support/validation pool of 512 images per class, fixed held-out test of 120 per class, no test-set access during selection, 20 distinct support-sampling trials), the selected configuration (the ViT-L-14 Vision Transformer encoder with OpenAI weights, 128 shots per class) reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.79 +/- 0.42% on the held-out test set; a label-efficient 16-shot setting, that is, 96 labeled support images at adaptation time across the six classes, already attains 90.17 +/- 0.81%. Tip-Adapter-F clearly outperforms both zero-shot CLIP and the standard training-free Tip-Adapter, and prompt and backbone analyses show that performance is stable across Vision Transformer encoders and insensitive to prompt wording at the selected operating point. Overall, CLIP visual features carry a transferable structure that a lightweight support cache turns into a label-efficient Phase-OTDR event classifier. The code and the corresponding image dataset are made publicly available on GitHub to support further research: https://github.com/miralab-ai/vlm-phase-otdr.

papers.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
papers.abstract_en: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

papers.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
papers.abstract_en: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

papers.title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual
papers.abstract_en: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).

papers.title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
papers.abstract_en: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at https://github.com/minhquoc0712/BECON.

papers.title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
papers.abstract_en: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
papers.abstract_en: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

papers.title: Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.

papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

papers.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
papers.abstract_en: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

papers.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
papers.abstract_en: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
papers.abstract_en: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

papers.title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
papers.abstract_en: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

papers.title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
papers.abstract_en: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/PPL-TSC.

papers.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
papers.abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

papers.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
papers.abstract_en: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

papers.title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
papers.abstract_en: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

papers.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
papers.abstract_en: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

papers.title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
papers.abstract_en: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

papers.title: Seeing Isn't Resolving: Visual and Linguistic Disambiguation with Conversational Grounding
papers.abstract_en: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.

papers.title: LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract_en: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.

papers.title: ScoutCache: Efficient Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Conditional Readout and Selective Caching
papers.abstract_en: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

papers.title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore
papers.abstract_en: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of "AI-generated" during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

papers.title: FaceJev: Direct Visual Decisions for Face Forgery Detection
papers.abstract_en: Face forgery detection methods often perform well on seen manipulations but generalize poorly to unseen ones. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can recognize facial parts and assess their visual plausibility. Existing MLLM-based methods typically express these judgments through textual explanations, but seldom treat individual part decisions as explicit learning targets. We present FaceJev, an MLLM-based method for face forgery detection through direct visual decisions. Following the Jev formulation, FaceJev answers eight independent questions about facial parts using a shared image encoding and reads anomaly probabilities from the native answer logits. A face is classified as forged if any part is predicted to be abnormal, directly linking the detection result to the part decisions. We construct PartForensics, a dataset of approximately 160k images with binary anomaly targets for the eight facial parts, to supervise these decisions. We further propose FS-GRPO, which optimizes each part decision through an exact reward comparison with its alternative, using both detection and part rewards. FaceJev outperforms the strongest baseline by 7.25 percentage points on unseen manipulations. Extensive ablation studies validate our design choices and the effectiveness of the main components.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
papers.abstract_en: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

papers.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
papers.abstract_en: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

papers.title: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
papers.abstract_en: Remote-sensing (RS) image scene classification aims to assign a semantic category to an overhead image, and in practice must often do so from only a handful of labelled examples, since annotation requires expert interpretation and the resulting labels transfer poorly across sensors and regions. Recent progress has come from adapting vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, through learned prompts or feature adapters. Although effective, these methods construct their representation entirely in the spatial domain. RS scenes are dominated by periodic texture and regular geometry, which the Fourier spectrum describes compactly through an amplitude component, carrying texture and contrast statistics, and a phase component, carrying spatial structure. Existing frequency-domain adaptation of VLMs either exploits amplitude alone or does not separate amplitude from phase, leaving the structural component unused. In this article, we propose PhaseCLIP, which inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder and trains only 1.30% of its parameters. Because the amplitude and phase pathways share an identical parameter layout, a single weight set is learned on phase and transferred exactly to amplitude, giving a two-stage scheme that adds no parameters. Experiments on five public RS datasets, EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS and RSSCN7, against eight baselines under a matched protocol, show that PhaseCLIP attains 84.28% mean accuracy and is the best method in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot cells, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the most difficult dataset. Because the modules act on the spectrum of image patches and transformer tokens and leave the text encoder untouched, the approach can be extended to other RS sensors and tasks, and to other domains in which class evidence lies in spatial structure.

papers.title: Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
papers.abstract_en: Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.

papers.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
papers.abstract_en: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.

papers.title: Glance, then Select: Evidence-Tempered Visual Token Selection for Extremely Compressed Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.

papers.title: Pixel is All You Need
papers.abstract_en: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

papers.title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
papers.abstract_en: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as distinct stages of a WSP pipeline.

papers.title: Syllable- and Word-Level Evaluation of Tibetan OCR
papers.abstract_en: Optical character recognition (OCR) for Tibetan is evaluated predominantly by character error rate (CER). Tibetan marks syllable boundaries but does not mark word boundaries, so a word error rate requires a segmenter. This study evaluates nine recognizer configurations on typeset, woodblock and two handwritten script styles, alone and in combination, and reports syllable- and word-level error rates, to our knowledge the first for Tibetan OCR. The configurations span CTC models, TrOCR encoder-decoders with and without post-training quantization, and a vision-language model, and each is scored under CER, the syllable error rate (SER) and three segmented word error rates (SWER). CER ranks systems largely as the higher-level rates do (Kendall $τ\geq 0.833$), with one pair ordered oppositely. On the effect of joint training, CER and SER record significant changes of opposite sign in 7 of 64 comparisons. SER needs no segmenter and ranks systems as SWER does under two of the three segmenters ($τ\geq 0.889$). The output of each configuration is also tagged for part of speech, annotated for named entities and machine translated, and each result is compared with that obtained on the reference text. As rough guidance, translation chrF of 60 is reached at SER of 0.047 or below and part-of-speech preservation of 0.8 at 0.078 or below, while no error rate separates the systems that reach entity preservation of 0.6 from those that do not.

papers.title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
papers.abstract_en: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

papers.title: Impact of Pretraining Length, Model Size, and Annotation Budget on Downstream Clinical Tasks of Foundation Models in Radiotherapy
papers.abstract_en: Cone-beam CT (CBCT) scans acquired during radiotherapy capture changes such as tumor shrinkage and radiation-induced tissue changes, offering great potential for foundation models that help monitor individual treatment responses. However, to our knowledge, no large-scale pretrained models for radiotherapy CBCT exist, and evaluating modeling choices is difficult since downstream tasks are not known in advance. We examine how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning strategy relate to downstream clinical performance, and how metrics tracked during pretraining correlate with it. We pretrain vision transformer encoders with masked image modeling on about 150,000 raw 3D radiotherapy CBCT scans, tracking representation quality via validation loss, effective rank, and linear probing. Downstream tasks are classification of feeding tube presence ($n=51,135$ CBCTs, $1,562$ patients) and clinical characteristics (T-, N-stage, sex, age, tumor site; $n=1,278$ patients) in head and neck cancer. We compare low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full finetuning against no pretraining, varying annotated dataset size. Pretext validation loss was the most consistent predictor of downstream performance; effective rank and linear probing were also associated, but not consistently across model sizes and finetuning methods. LoRA performed comparably to full finetuning while training only 0.5-2.5% of the parameters. Fully finetuned models consistently outperformed models without pretraining across all sizes, with AUROC 0.91-0.97 vs. 0.58-0.85 for feeding tube classification and 0.99-1.00 vs. 0.71-0.97 for sex classification. Model size had only a small, inconsistent effect, suggesting smaller models suffice at lower computational cost. papers.title: How to Explain your Unexplainable Video Anomaly Detector
papers.abstract_en: Weakly-supervised Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) models assign anomaly scores from high-dimensional features, and their predictions remain unexplained. Saliency maps show where a model looks but not what it relies on, and the descriptions produced by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are generated by branches that the anomaly score never reads. To address this faithfulness gap, we propose \textbf{Explain The Unexplainable (ETU)}, a classifier-agnostic framework that audits frozen VAD models through counterfactual interventions in their feature space. ETU maps video features to a discrete dependency graph of agents, actions and outcomes ($A_r \to A_a \to A_o$), regenerates the features by graph-conditioned diffusion with selected nodes of the graph masked, and measures the change in the score of a frozen detector; one set of interventions is applied unchanged to every detector. The generator is trained only to reconstruct the input features, so it cannot learn the contrast it is asked to measure, and we validate the audit with experiments that test every alternative explanation of its results, from the cost of regeneration to random deletions of matched size. On UCF-Crime features obtained from a CLIP encoder, we show that substituting the scene semantics results in the largest drop for most detectors, and that removing the outcome chain of the graph ($Δ_{rel}$) changes the anomaly score of all six audited detectors far more than removing the same number of random nodes, even though the random deletion perturbs the features about as much. We show that this targeted behavior comes from the divergence objective of the graph embedding. Without it, the two interventions become indistinguishable, and with a divergence objective in the generator as well, the score change of the detector follows the displacement of the reconstruction rather than the semantics that were removed.

papers.title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
papers.abstract_en: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.

papers.title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.

papers.title: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
papers.abstract_en: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.

papers.title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract_en: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.

papers.title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
papers.abstract_en: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

papers.title: Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
papers.abstract_en: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.

papers.title: MedicalDPO: Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization for CT to PET Translation
papers.abstract_en: CT-to-PET synthesis estimates functional PET images from anatomical CT scans for auxiliary analysis, representation pretraining, and missing-modality completion. Brownian Bridge diffusion models can produce multiple PET candidates of different quality under the same CT condition, exposing an intra-condition quality hierarchy. Candidate quality spans complementary spatial, structural, and intensity dimensions, while DPO-only fine-tuning may compromise absolute synthesis fidelity. We propose MedicalDPO which converts this hierarchy into preference supervision automatically constructed from paired CT-PET training data. Multiple candidates are ranked across the three fidelity dimensions, and strict cross-metric verification retains preferred-rejected pairs with consistent quality separation. Relative denoising-error preference optimization is jointly trained with the original Brownian Bridge objective to anchor the pretrained CT-to-PET mapping, while condition-balanced multi-pair rotation distributes preference supervision across CT conditions. Experiments on BBDM and CPDM show improvements across LPIPS, MAE, SSIM, and PSNR. Further analyses demonstrate metric complementarity and clear pair separation, while ablations show that the original training objective prevents the substantial degradation caused by DPO-only fine-tuning.

papers.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
papers.abstract_en: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
