papers.title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
papers.abstract_en: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

papers.title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
papers.abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

papers.title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
papers.abstract_en: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.abstract_en: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

papers.title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
papers.abstract_en: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

papers.title: Keeping Parts Honest: Isolated Part Graphs for Faithful Vision Transformer Explanations
papers.abstract_en: Part and prototype-based explanations for Vision Transformers (ViTs) present a decision as evidence from individual image regions. However, self-attention mixes information across patches, so part-level features absorb context from the whole image and consequently fail to faithfully reflect the decision. We show that existing interpretable ViT classifiers depend heavily on this leakage: when each explained region is encoded in isolation, their accuracy collapses, and retraining them under isolation recovers only part of the lost accuracy. We propose a classifier that represents each image as a graph of isolated parts. Each part is encoded only from its own patches by a ViT whose last blocks are fine-tuned under isolation, preventing evidence leakage from elsewhere in the image. Parts are discovered without annotation and refined hierarchically through their sub-parts, making them more consistent and stable across images than those of competing methods. Each edge is computed from part pairs, and recovers evidence that attention previously shared across the object without affecting the parts. Matching the image graph to a learned prototype graph per class makes the prediction a direct combination of node and edge similarities, each computed only from the patches it is credited to, so every explanation is faithful by construction. Across 11 fine-grained and general-object benchmarks, our method exceeds the accuracy of existing explainable methods that rely on leakage, while providing explanations that reflect what the model actually uses.

papers.title: DuoFlow: Towards Synchronized Speech and Motion Generation with Fine-Grained Control
papers.abstract_en: An embodied speaker's expressiveness depends not only on what is said, but also on how the voice sounds and how the body moves. However, existing joint speech-motion generation models are largely driven implicitly by transcript semantics or intermediate speech representations, offering little explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, or vocal style. To bridge this gap, we construct MotionSpeech, a structured benchmark for controllable joint speech-motion generation that includes transcripts, voice-style descriptions, and motion conditions at two hierarchical levels. Building on this benchmark, we propose DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer that jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and a unified second-based temporal coordinate. Modality-specific residual connectors inject structured conditions into the corresponding streams, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention coordinates their generation, and a monotonic phoneme pathway combines normalized progress anchors with CTC supervision to strengthen speech temporal modeling. DuoFlow provides a unified interface for fine-grained motion and vocal-style control and demonstrates the ability to synthesize high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences. Project page, https://jundong-dev.github.io/DuoFlow-project-page.

papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.abstract_en: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

papers.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
papers.abstract_en: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.abstract_en: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

papers.title: GRAZE: Text-Free Grasp Synthesis for Unseen Objects from Human Gaze
papers.abstract_en: Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generation provides intuitive semantic control, but language is an indirect way to specify where an interaction should occur on an object. Naming the part to grasp requires object-specific words, and naming the approach side requires a reference frame that a prompt lacks. We propose GRAZE (GRAsp from gaZE), which generates hand-object grasp motion from recorded gaze instead of object and part names. Its Geometry-Aware Gaze Encoding (GeoGaze) maps gaze rays to cues on object geometry, and cross-attention conditions a diffusion Transformer on these cues. We also introduce HOT3D-Grasp, a grasp-centered benchmark with object-disjoint folds built on HOT3D recordings. On unseen objects, GRAZE grasps the target part more often than the strongest text-conditioned baseline (49.3% vs. 43.6%), achieves the highest grasp success (66.3% vs. 46.6%), and transfers without fine-tuning to GazeHOI (45.3% vs. 33.8%). Gaze conveys the approach side: when gaze is rotated around the object, the approach turns with it in 59.1% of cases, against 20.5% for a text model retrained with clock words. On the same backbone, a text prompt names parts better, but gaze adds the approach side. Given both, GRAZE keeps the prompt's part accuracy and follows gaze.

papers.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
papers.abstract_en: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

papers.title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
papers.abstract_en: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.

papers.title: Learning a Task-Adaptive Low-Dimensional Semantic Space for Improved Visual Classification
papers.abstract_en: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
papers.abstract_en: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

papers.title: MT-RGCN-DTI: A Multi-Task Relational Graph Convolutional Network for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract_en: Prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) has become a very crucial part of drug discovery. With the increase in the data volume, it has become very important to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple data sources. In this regard, utilising multiple resources in the form of heterogeneous information network to address DTI prediction can be rewarding. In this work, we propose a heterogeneous information network based multi-task DTI prediction model which leverages the advantages of relation graph convolutional network (RGCN). To achieve this, the model employs drug-target interaction network, drug-drug similarity network and protein-protein similarity network to construct a heterogeneous information network. Moreover, we use a knowledge graph embedding scoring functions to model interactions between drug and targets, specifically DistMult and ComplEx as decoders over the learned node representations. We performed extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. We observed that the proposed model shows competitive performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/Dheeran-S/MT-RGCN-DTI/.

papers.title: $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
papers.abstract_en: $π^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $π^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.

papers.title: Synergizing Evidence Retrieval and Utilization for Self-Improving Multimodal Scientific Document Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.

papers.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
papers.abstract_en: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

papers.title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
papers.abstract_en: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.abstract_en: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

papers.title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
papers.abstract_en: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
papers.abstract_en: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

papers.title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
papers.abstract_en: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.

papers.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
papers.abstract_en: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

papers.title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
papers.abstract_en: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

papers.title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
papers.abstract_en: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home

papers.title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
papers.abstract_en: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.

papers.title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements
papers.abstract_en: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.

papers.title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
papers.abstract_en: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
papers.abstract_en: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

papers.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract_en: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

papers.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
papers.abstract_en: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

papers.title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract_en: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

papers.title: AdaModalX: Synchronization-Free MFM Inference for Distributed Multimodal Mobile Sensing via Progressive Data Orchestration
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.

papers.title: Structure-Guided Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer for Efficient Monocular 3D Human Pose Estimation
papers.abstract_en: Existing multi-granularity methods for monocular 3D human pose estimation emphasize spatial joint features while underusing skeletal structure, including global connectivity and temporal continuity. Moreover, modeling entire frame sequences incurs high computational costs. We propose a Structure-Aware Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer that integrates structural priors across spatial and temporal representations for accurate and efficient pose estimation. A three-level feature extractor captures human topology at the joint, bone, and limb levels. Gated Adaptive Spatial Attention (GASA) embeds structural constraints into spatial attention, while Multi-Granularity Feature Enhancement (MGFE) uses hierarchical pooling and fusion to strengthen local details and global semantics. Temporal Segment Fusion (TSF) aligns temporal contexts across granularities to capture both short- and long-range motion patterns. Hierarchical Cross-Attention (HCA) promotes spatiotemporal interaction between granularities, and Keyframe Attention (KFA) selects informative motion segments to reduce redundancy and computational cost. Experiments demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional Transformer-based approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of structure-aware multi-granularity modeling for monocular 3D human pose estimation.

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
papers.abstract_en: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

papers.title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
papers.abstract_en: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.

papers.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
papers.abstract_en: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

papers.title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract_en: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $Θ(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}α\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

papers.title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
papers.abstract_en: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

papers.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

papers.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

papers.title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
papers.abstract_en: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

papers.title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
papers.abstract_en: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

papers.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
papers.abstract_en: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

papers.title: Beyond Family Labels: A Taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Prior for Avian 3D Shape Recovery
papers.abstract_en: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.

papers.title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
papers.abstract_en: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

papers.title: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
papers.abstract_en: Motor imagery (MI) enables a brain-computer interface (BCI) to decode movement intentions without overt movement. Hybrid electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) classification combines complementary signals, but inter-subject variability and the design of information exchange between modalities affect generalization to new subjects. We propose a framework that combines Cross-Subject Class Mixup (CSCM) with Selective Attention. CSCM aims to construct new training data to make the model robust against inter-subject variability. It independently selects EEG and fNIRS donor trials from other training subjects within the anchor class and mixes each modality while preserving the original label. Selective Attention provides an effective way to simultaneously model the temporal signal characteristics and fuse the two modalities. It retains causal temporal self-attention for EEG and uses a classification token (CLS) to integrate both modalities, without fNIRS attention updates or direct cross-modal temporal-token attention. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation across 28 subjects on a public EEG-fNIRS dataset yields a mean balanced accuracy (BA) of 76.85% and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 76.58%. The proposed model achieves the highest mean performance among five reimplemented baselines. We also examine the contributions of CSCM and Selective Attention through modality-specific mixing and donor-policy comparisons, temporal-policy comparisons, interventions on direct cross-modal paths, and component ablations.

papers.title: AFRNet: Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for Image Deraining
papers.abstract_en: Image deraining aims to recover rain-free images from rain-degraded observations. Recent frequency-aware deraining methods have demonstrated promising performance by removing rain artifacts in the spectral domain. However, since rain artifacts and background textures often appear in several correlated subbands, prior frequency-domain deraining models still enhance frequency subbands separately. Such band-wise processing limits information exchange across subbands. Without context from other subbands, rain and clean content that appear together in one subband cannot be separated. This leads to either residual rain streaks or over-smoothing of fine details. To address this limitation, we propose AFRNet, an Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for image deraining. First, we introduce an Adaptive Frequency Recombination Module (AFRM) that performs cross-band modulation among wavelet subbands, enabling information interaction and adaptive recombination of degraded frequency components. We then develop a Subband Compensation Block (SCB) that compensates for decoder subband degradation by leveraging encoder subband features through inter-subband attention in the wavelet domain, alleviating detail loss during reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AFRNet achieves competitive performance and consistent results across diverse deraining benchmarks.
